claims.text: The starting eutectic high-entropy alloy has a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies.
The untreated alloy has limited room-temperature tensile ductility and exhibits brittle failure.
Dislocation pile-ups at internal dual-phase lamellar boundaries cause local stress concentrations, microcrack initiation, and brittle failure in the untreated alloy.
A controlled, short-duration annealing or aging treatment near the order-disorder transition temperature will trigger nanoscale precipitate formation at lamellar interfaces.
The heat treatment will produce coherent precipitates localized along the internal lamellar boundaries.
The boundary precipitates will act as effective dislocation sinks.
The precipitates will facilitate smoother dislocation transmission across lamellar interfaces.
Smoother dislocation transmission will reduce dislocation accumulation at the interfaces.
Reduced dislocation accumulation will lower local stress concentrations.
Lower local stress concentrations will mitigate microcrack initiation and catastrophic brittle failure.
The heat-treated alloy will have at least about 20% greater elongation to failure than the untreated alloy at room temperature.
The heat-treated alloy will maintain or slightly increase yield strength relative to the untreated alloy.
The heat-treated alloy will maintain or slightly increase ultimate tensile strength relative to the untreated alloy.
An inert treatment atmosphere will avoid oxidation during heat treatment.
The predicted mechanical-property benefits apply to room-temperature, quasi-static tensile loading.
Overaging may coarsen the precipitates.
Deviation from the optimal heat-treatment temperature may cause unwanted phase transformations.
Precipitate coarsening or unwanted phase transformations may compromise the alloy's mechanical properties.
The quantitative ductility and strength gains depend on the exact heat-treatment conditions.
The quantitative ductility and strength gains depend on the alloy composition.
